stem: A statement of affairs is used to find a trader's …

options.rationale: Correct: assets less liabilities on that date equal capital.
Revenue comes from a reconstructed income statement, not from a list of assets and liabilities.
Receipts come from a cash and bank summary.
A statement of affairs shows no trading figures at all.

explanation: The statement of affairs applies the accounting equation at one date: capital = assets − liabilities.

stem: Which is a **disadvantage** of keeping incomplete records?

options.content: No trial balance can be drawn up to check the arithmetic
options.rationale: Correct: without double entry there is no arithmetical check.

options.content: The records cost little to keep
options.rationale: Low cost is an advantage of incomplete records.

options.content: The owner needs little bookkeeping knowledge
options.rationale: This is an advantage, not a disadvantage.

options.content: Records can be kept quickly by the owner
options.rationale: Speed is an advantage.

explanation: Incomplete records are cheap and simple, but there is no trial balance, little detail and theft is hard to detect.

stem: Tatenda's capital was US\$8,420 on 1 January 2025 and US\$11,150 on 31 December 2025. His drawings for the year were US\$5,200. What was his profit for the year?

options.rationale: This is only the increase in capital; drawings have not been added back.
Drawings have been deducted instead of added back.
The two capitals have been added instead of compared.

explanation: Profit = closing capital − opening capital + drawings = 11,150 − 8,420 + 5,200 = 7,930.

stem: Thandeka's capital rose from US\$15,600 to US\$18,900 during 2025. She took drawings of US\$3,800 and paid US\$5,000 of her savings into the business. What was the profit for the year?

options.rationale: Capital introduced has been added instead of deducted.
Capital introduced has been ignored, so the savings are counted as profit.
The signs of drawings and capital introduced have been swapped.

hints: Add back what the owner took out; take away what the owner put in.

stem: In a statement of affairs, how is a **bank overdraft** shown?

options.rationale: An overdraft is money owed, not money held.
Correct: the business owes the bank this amount.
An overdraft is repayable on demand, so it is current.

options.content: As a deduction from capital introduced
options.rationale: It is a liability of the business, not an owner item.

explanation: An overdraft is a short-term debt to the bank: a current liability.

stem: On 1 January 2025 Sipho's carpentry business had: van US\$6,500, inventory US\$2,340, trade receivables US\$1,170, cash US\$260; trade payables US\$1,890 and rent owing US\$150. What was his capital?

options.rationale: Rent owing has been added as an asset instead of deducted as a liability.
This is total assets; liabilities have not been deducted.
The van has been left out: non-current assets are part of capital.
Correct: assets 10,270 − liabilities 2,040.

explanation: Assets 10,270 − liabilities 2,040 = 8,230.

stem: A trader's capital fell during the year, yet the business made a profit. Which explains this?

options.rationale: Capital introduced would increase capital, not reduce it.

options.content: Drawings were greater than the profit
options.rationale: Correct: taking out more than was earned reduces capital.

options.content: Inventory at the year end was higher
options.rationale: Higher inventory increases assets and capital.

options.content: Trade payables at the year end were lower
options.rationale: Lower liabilities increase capital.

explanation: Closing capital = opening + profit − drawings (+ capital introduced). If drawings exceed profit, capital falls even though there was a profit.
hints: Closing capital = opening capital + profit + capital introduced − drawings.

stem: During the year Chipo took goods costing US\$480 from her shop for her family, as well as cash drawings. How are the goods treated when profit is found from the change in capital?

options.content: They are deducted as capital introduced
options.rationale: Capital introduced is resources put in, not taken out.

options.content: They are added to the cash drawings and added back
options.rationale: Correct: goods taken are drawings at cost.

options.content: They are ignored because no cash changed hands
options.rationale: Any asset taken for private use is drawings.

options.content: They are added to closing inventory
options.rationale: The goods have left the business, so they are not inventory.

explanation: Goods taken for private use reduce the business's assets, so they are drawings and must be added back with the cash drawings.
hints: Drawings can be cash, goods or other assets.

stem: What does the change-in-capital method **not** tell the owner?

options.content: Whether the business made a profit or a loss
options.rationale: This is exactly what the method finds.

options.content: The capital at the end of the year
options.rationale: The closing statement of affairs shows it.

options.content: How much gross profit was made on sales
options.rationale: Correct: the method gives only the overall profit or loss.

options.content: The total value of assets at the year end
options.rationale: The closing statement of affairs lists them.

explanation: Comparing capitals gives one figure. There is no revenue, cost of sales or list of expenses, so the owner cannot see how the profit arose.

stem: Expenses paid in advance at the year end are listed as a current asset in the statement of affairs.
explanation: True. A prepayment is a benefit the business has paid for but not yet used: an asset.

stem: Money lent to the business by the owner's brother is treated as capital introduced.
explanation: False. A loan from anyone other than the owner is a liability of the business. Only resources put in by the owner are capital introduced.

stem: Match each item with where it belongs when a trader's profit is found from the change in capital.

left.content: A legacy paid into the business by the owner

right.content: Asset in the statement of affairs
Liability in the statement of affairs
Added back to the change in capital
Deducted from the change in capital

explanation: Prepayments and receivables are assets; accruals and overdrafts are liabilities; drawings (cash or goods) are added back; capital introduced is deducted.

stem: Complete the formula.

payload.template: Profit for the year = closing capital − opening capital {{blank:a}} drawings {{blank:b}} capital introduced.

explanation: Drawings are added back because they reduced closing capital; capital introduced is deducted because it increased closing capital without being earned.

stem: Nyasha's transport business had capital of US\$23,480 at 1 January 2025 and US\$21,790 at 31 December 2025. During the year she withdrew US\$6,300 and paid in US\$1,500 from the sale of a private plot. Calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: Change in capital 21,790 − 23,480 = (1,690) (a fall). Add drawings 6,300: 4,610. Less capital introduced 1,500: profit 3,110. Using only the change in capital suggests a loss of 1,690; adding the capital introduced gives 6,110.
workedSolution: 1. Change in capital 21,790 − 23,480 = (1,690) (a fall). Add drawings 6,300: 4,610. Less capital introduced 1,500: profit 3,110. Using only the change in capital suggests a loss of 1,690; adding the capital introduced gives 6,110.
hints: Capital fell, but drawings were large. Adjust the change in capital for both owner items.

stem: Rudo's opening capital was US\$9,750. Her profit for the year was US\$6,420 and her drawings US\$4,880. Calculate her closing capital.
explanation: Closing capital = 9,750 + 6,420 − 4,880 = 11,290. Adding the drawings gives 21,050.
workedSolution: 1. Closing capital = 9,750 + 6,420 − 4,880 = 11,290. Adding the drawings gives 21,050.

stem: Farai's records were destroyed in a fire. His accountant knows that his capital at 31 December 2025 was US\$14,260, his profit for 2025 was US\$5,130 and his drawings were US\$3,970. No capital was introduced. Calculate Farai's capital at 1 January 2025.
explanation: Opening = closing − profit + drawings = 14,260 − 5,130 + 3,970 = 13,100. Deducting the drawings as well gives 5,160.
workedSolution: 1. Opening = closing − profit + drawings = 14,260 − 5,130 + 3,970 = 13,100. Deducting the drawings as well gives 5,160.
hints: Start from closing = opening + profit − drawings and rearrange.

stem: Give **two** reasons why the owner of a small market stall may keep incomplete records.

points.description: Full double-entry records take too much time / the owner lacks bookkeeping knowledge
A bookkeeper or accountant costs money the business cannot afford / few transactions so detail seems unnecessary

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She has no training in double entry and is busy selling, and she cannot afford to pay a bookkeeper for a business with so few transactions.

explanation: Time, knowledge and cost are the usual reasons.

stem: Sipho calculates his profit each year from the change in capital. Advise him whether he should start keeping a full set of double-entry records. Give **two** reasons and a conclusion.

points.description: Double entry gives a trial balance check on accuracy / helps detect theft or errors
It shows detail: revenue, gross profit and each expense, so costs can be controlled; lenders prefer it
Conclusion weighed against cost/time (e.g. he should, if the business is growing or needs a loan)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Full records would let him prepare a trial balance, so errors and missing cash would be found, and an income statement would show which expenses are rising. A bank would also accept the figures more readily. Although they take more time or a bookkeeper's fee, he should change if he plans to grow or borrow.

explanation: A balanced answer weighs detail and control against cost and time.
hints: Think about what the change-in-capital method cannot show.
